# Elementary English Reading Program

The study followed 240 students for two full school years [1].

Teachers measured reading progress every six weeks with a short test.

Students who read daily improved faster than the others [2].

The effect was largest for students who started behind.

Parents received a short guide about reading at home [3].

Most families used the guide at least once a week.

Reading scores rose by twelve points on average across the group [1].

The control group improved by only four points.

Attendance also improved in the reading group [2].

Students reported enjoying reading more than before.

The program cost about forty dollars per student [4].

Staff training took one afternoon and used existing materials.

Three other schools copied the program the next year [5].

All three saw similar gains in reading scores.

The researchers checked results by student age and gender.

Gains held for every group they examined [3].

Students kept reading during the summer break [2].

The summer slide was much smaller than in past years.

Teachers said the weekly check was easy to run.

Ninety percent of teachers would run it again [4].

The team published the full data set online [1].

Anyone can download the data and check the numbers.

A second study in another state copied the design.

The results matched closely across both states [5].

Costs stayed low because schools already owned the books.

The program runs with one teacher and a small shelf.

Reading time replaced silent study, not core lessons.

Parents asked for the same guide in two more languages.

The school translated the guide over one weekend.

Math scores did not change in either group [3].

The researchers plan a five year follow up study.

They will report again when students finish middle school.
